Assessment.Summary: The scene effectively establishes the protagonist's selfish, utilitarian voice and tactical competence, but it suffers from significant redundancy in its internal monologue. The narrative repeatedly explains the protagonist's intent to use Miller as a shield and his view of Miller as a tool, diluting the impact of the characterization. Additionally, the prose relies on a repetitive sentence structure ("I was the one who...") that creates a monotonous rhythm and feels like forced emphasis rather than natural thought.

Findings.Explanation: The prose repeatedly states the protagonist's intent to use Miller as a shield and his view of Miller as a utility. E3 explicitly states Miller is a "fleshy shield" and that efficiency is the only religion. E6 explains that safety makes men obedient. E8 describes the "transaction" and the protagonist's experience versus Miller's inexperience. E9 compares the compliment to a mechanic assessing a car's utility. E10 explains that Miller's hesitation keeps him in the protagonist's shadow where he is useful. This constant re-explanation of the same dynamic prevents the reader from inferring the character's nature through action and instead feels like the author is lecturing the reader on the protagonist's morality.
Findings.RevisionGuidance: Trim the internal monologue that explicitly defines the relationship as exploitative or transactional. Allow the actions (positioning Miller, the specific wording of orders, the physical hauling) to demonstrate the dynamic. Remove the explanatory sentences that tell the reader what the protagonist thinks about Miller's utility, letting the reader draw the conclusion from the behavior.
EvidenceQuotes: That was a lie, of course. I had the sector because I had positioned myself so that his body was the primary barrier between me and the open ground. He was a fleshy shield, a human sandbag that happened to know how to aim a weapon. It was efficient. In the field, efficiency was the only religion that mattered. If you could use a man’s fear to keep him quiet and his body to keep you alive, you were a good soldier. If you wasted that potential on sympathy, you were a liability.

He nodded, his eyes wide and wet. He wanted to believe me. He wanted to believe that I was a leader, a protector, a guy who had his back covered. I let him have that. It was easier to control a man who felt safe than one who felt afraid. Fear made men unpredictable. Safety made them obedient.

Rotation. That meant we were moving. That meant the next wave of men would take our place in the ditch, and we would move forward into the open. I looked at Miller. He looked at me. In that look, I saw the transaction. I was the one with the plan. I was the one with the experience. I was the one who had survived the last three rotations. He was the one who was about to find out what it felt like to be on the other side of the line.
"Good job, Miller," I said, and I meant it in the way that a mechanic means it when he tells a driver his car is in good shape. It was a compliment to the utility, not the soul.

I started to crawl out of the ditch, my movements practiced and silent. I didn’t look back. I knew he would follow. I knew he would look at the open ground and feel the pull of the enemy’s guns, and I knew he would hesitate. That hesitation was what I needed. It would keep him behind me, in my shadow, where he was useful.

Findings.Explanation: The final paragraphs (E19, E20) rely on a repetitive anaphoric structure ("I was the one who...") that feels mechanical and overly emphatic. This pattern disrupts the natural flow of the first-person voice and comes across as forced dramatic emphasis rather than organic thought.
Findings.RevisionGuidance: Vary the sentence structure in the concluding lines. Instead of repeating the "I was the one who" construction, use distinct sentences that reflect the protagonist's immediate physical state and intent without the repetitive rhetorical device.
EvidenceQuotes: I stood up, brushing the mud from my uniform. I was clean. I was ready. I was the one who had made the move. I was the one who had taken the risk. I was the one who had survived.
And I was the one who was about to go back out there and do it again.
